title: The Extended Mind: Why Did You Do It or Did the AI? Is the Wrong Question
author: Anthea Roberts

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI writing: Present gains can weaken future judgment
st.an: Roberts supports supervised augmentation by insisting that humans retain genuine higher-level direction rather than passively delegating both tactical and strategic thinking. She also acknowledges cognitive-atrophy evidence, while arguing that selective offloading can strengthen strategic cognition rather than necessarily weaken judgment.
qs: A paper published in *Frontiers in AI* in 2025 — titled "The Extended Hollowed Mind" — warned that AI can simultaneously extend cognition and cause cognitive atrophy.
It's whether you're genuinely operating at the higher level — or just sitting back while the AI does both.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Roberts supports the cluster’s core augmentation thesis by portraying agentic AI as incorporated into a collaborative human cognitive process rather than as a wholesale substitute for human thinking. Her account reinforces human–AI co-creation, though it does not address the cluster’s operational claims about jagged capability, verification, task selection or workflow redesign.
qs: Because as somebody who works closely with agentic AI, almost everything about it is co-created.

kp.k: Human–AI co-creation challenges individual attribution models
kp.d: Roberts argues that separating human thinking from AI contribution misrepresents her iterative research practice. She challenges assumptions underlying student evaluation, originality and authorship that cognition is an individual performance and external assistance necessarily compromises credit. This is a conceptual argument grounded in her experience, not a measured finding about professional outcomes.
qs: Because as somebody who works closely with agentic AI, almost everything about it is co-created.
This assumption runs deep. It's in how we evaluate students, how we assess originality, how we assign authorship.
So when people ask the question "did you write it, or did the AI?", my reaction is that we both wrote it and that the framing of the question is wrong.

kp.k: Extended cognition supplies a framework for AI collaboration
kp.d: Roberts draws on Annie Murphy Paul's account of embodied, situated and distributed cognition and Clark and Chalmers's 1998 extended-mind argument. She reports Clark's May 2025 Nature Communications paper as extending this framework to AI: technologies participate in hybrid cognitive systems rather than simply replacing individual thought. These are attributed theoretical claims supporting her interpretation of AI use.
qs: Her argument, grounded in decades of work by cognitive scientists and philosophers, is that the mind does not stop at the skull.
Their argument: when an external resource plays the same functional role that an internal cognitive process would play, it IS part of your cognitive system. Not metaphorically. Literally.
New technologies don't replace our thinking. They create what he calls "delicately interwoven new wholes" — brain, body, and world working together, each adapting to what the rest offers.

kp.k: Writing offers a historical analogy for cognitive trade-offs
kp.d: Invoking Socrates's warning about writing in Plato's Phaedrus, around 370 BC, Roberts argues that a tool can weaken one capacity while enabling more complex thought and intergenerational accumulation of knowledge. Her claims about writing and memory serve as a historical analogy for AI, not direct evidence of AI's effects.
qs: In Plato's *Phaedrus*, written around 370 BC, Socrates warned that the invention of writing would destroy human memory.
Writing didn't make us stupider. It did make our memories worse. But it also made a different kind of thinking possible — thinking that was more complex than an individual could hold in their head.
And writing this complex thinking down also meant that thinking could be passed more easily down the generations, so one person's thought could be built more easily on top of another's.

kp.k: Go evidence suggests AI can expand human novelty
kp.d: Roberts reports a study discussed in Clark's paper finding greater novelty in human Go moves following the emergence of superhuman AI strategies. She interprets this as creative extension beyond established conventions rather than imitation. The document supplies no sample size, effect magnitude or study period, and the finding concerns Go rather than legal work.
qs: A study of human Go players found that following the emergence of superhuman AI playing strategies, human players showed *more* novelty in their own moves — not less.
They broke past centuries of received wisdom and began exploring parts of the game that had been invisible to them.

kp.k: Research agents support synthesis, exploration and critical dialogue
kp.d: Roberts describes encoding her frameworks and methods into agents, directing background research, supplying theses, drafting orally and repeatedly editing. She identifies three benefits in her own practice: higher-level synthesis, interdisciplinary exploration and directed challenge. Her example tracks nine competing AI narratives week over week; these are self-reported capabilities, not comparative productivity measurements.
qs: I have created the agents I interact with by encoding my cognitive frameworks and methodological approaches into them and their skills.
I extensively edit and reframe — I am currently on version 14 of my essay on AI and competing narratives.
Ascending — operating at a higher level of synthesis than a single mind can sustain. Nine competing narratives about AI, their champions, their evidence, their interactions, tracked week over week.
Exploring — pushing across disciplinary boundaries that my training doesn't span.
Collaborating — thinking with a partner who can be directed to challenge me from perspectives I'm inclined to overlook.

kp.k: Reported cognitive-debt findings complicate the extension argument
kp.d: Roberts reports that the 2025 Frontiers in AI paper "The Extended Hollowed Mind" warns that AI can extend cognition while causing atrophy. That paper cites a study showing up to a 55% reduction in cortical activity during AI-assisted writing, accompanied by memory impairment. Roberts takes the concern seriously but disputes whether reduced engagement with task-level detail necessarily demonstrates diminished higher-level thinking. No sample size or methodological detail is supplied.
qs: A paper published in *Frontiers in AI* in 2025 — titled "The Extended Hollowed Mind" — warned that AI can simultaneously extend cognition and cause cognitive atrophy.
The authors point to a study showing up to a 55% reduction in cortical activity during AI-assisted writing, accompanied by memory impairment.
The underlying study calls this "cognitive debt" — short-term efficiency purchased at the expense of deeper encoding.
I take this seriously. But I think the framing misses something that becomes obvious if you think about how teams already work.

kp.k: Legal-team delegation illustrates strategic ascent rather than atrophy
kp.d: Using her husband's legal-team leadership as an anecdotal analogy, Roberts describes juniors researching cases and drafting while the leader directs strategy, interrogates and revises drafts, requests further work and signs off. She argues that reduced recall of quotations and citations can accompany greater strategic attention rather than cognitive atrophy. She applies this collective-work model to human–AI teams without presenting evidence of profession-wide adoption or staffing changes.
qs: My husband leads legal teams. He directs the strategy and assigns writing tasks to juniors. They're the ones who read the underlying cases and produce the first draft.
He interrogates those drafts, revises them, and has enough background to know whether the research sounds right or is off.
When he is happy with the final output, he signs off on it. Literally.
He has ascended up the scale to do the directing, the coaching, and the editing.
The difference now is that the teams aren't just humans working together. They're humans and AI working together.

kp.k: Active supervision separates extension from passive offloading
kp.d: Roberts recommends judging AI use by whether it improves thinking and whether the user continues directing, questioning, editing and challenging outputs. She argues that strategic delegation only counts as extension when the human genuinely performs higher-level work. Her expectation that users will diverge into cognitively active and passive groups is explicitly speculative and conditional on practice.
qs: The real question isn't whether you know less at one level. It's whether you're genuinely operating at the higher level — or just sitting back while the AI does both.
Going forward, I suspect we're going to see cognitive gym bunnies and cognitive couch potatoes. The technology is the same. The outcomes diverge based on how you use it.
Instead of "did I do it or did the AI?" — ask whether you're thinking better with this tool than without it.
Extension means you're still in it — directing, questioning, editing, pushing back. Offloading means you've stepped out.

kp.k: AI delegation raises an unresolved apprenticeship problem
kp.d: Roberts identifies foundational expertise as a condition of effective agent direction: her husband's ability to detect problems in briefs rests on years of granular legal work, and her own agent supervision draws on decades of research training. She asks how students and junior analysts will develop judgment if AI enables them to bypass argument construction and apprenticeship. She treats this as an unresolved, potentially central training challenge rather than an established outcome or a problem for which she offers a solution.
qs: But there's a second question that may matter even more: how do you develop the expertise and taste to direct agents well in the first place?
My husband can smell when something is off in a brief because he spent years doing the granular work himself.
I can direct AI agents effectively because I have decades of research training to draw on.
What happens to the people who never build that foundation — the students who reach for AI before they've learned to construct an argument, the junior analysts who skip the hard apprenticeship years?
That's a question I'm exploring in a forthcoming piece on the training crisis, and I think it may be the most consequential challenge the extended mind faces in an AI world.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Roberts argues that actively directed AI use expands research and thinking capacity through higher-level synthesis, cross-disciplinary exploration and interactive challenge.
pts.d: This is principally a cross-domain argument about research and professional cognition, rather than a prediction about legal-market economics. Roberts describes AI-assisted drafting as co-creation: she supplies frameworks, topics and initial theses, directs research, develops ideas orally, and repeatedly edits and reframes outputs. She claims that this interaction enables synthesis beyond what one person can hold simultaneously, exploration outside the user's training, and engagement with perspectives the user might otherwise overlook.

pts.k: Roberts presents human–AI work as an extension of professional teamwork, potentially shifting human effort toward strategy, direction, questioning and editing rather than detailed first-draft production.
pts.d: Her legal example is her husband's supervision of human juniors, used as an analogy for human–AI collaboration, not as evidence that his legal team has replaced juniors with AI. She argues that lower recall of underlying details need not constitute cognitive atrophy if the professional is genuinely exercising higher-level judgment. Her preferred model is augmentation with an actively involved human, not unattended reliance on AI.

pts.k: Roberts predicts divergent cognitive outcomes from AI use and identifies the development of foundational expertise as a potentially consequential training challenge.
pts.d: She distinguishes active cognitive extension from disengaged offloading and predicts that the same technology will benefit or weaken users differently depending on practice. She also raises, rather than resolves, the question of how novices will acquire the judgment needed to direct agents if they bypass argument construction and granular apprenticeship work. This is a conditional concern about students and junior professionals, not a quantified forecast of legal employment or training outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The positive capability claims rest on Roberts's personal research practice, an analogy to legal supervision, extended-mind scholarship and a reported study of human Go players.
pts.d: Roberts describes configuring agents with her methodologies, directing background research and undertaking extensive revision. Her account of her husband's legal supervision illustrates strategic delegation rather than measuring AI performance in legal work. She invokes Annie Murphy Paul's synthesis of cognition research, Clark and Chalmers's 1998 extended-mind argument, and Clark's May 2025 Nature Communications paper. She reports that a Go study discussed by Clark found greater novelty in human moves after superhuman AI strategies emerged, using this as support for creative extension. The document supplies no legal-service productivity data or quantified assessment of her own workflow.

pts.k: Roberts acknowledges reported empirical evidence of cognitive costs, while her predictions about divergent outcomes and novice training are grounded in interpretation and professional experience.
pts.d: She reports that the 2025 Frontiers in AI paper 'The Extended Hollowed Mind' cites an underlying study showing up to a 55% reduction in cortical activity during AI-assisted writing, accompanied by memory impairment. This is a secondhand report of a study, not Roberts's own finding or a legal-work benchmark. She takes the warning seriously but questions whether reduced engagement with detail necessarily means atrophy when higher-level work increases. Her training concern draws on the years of granular legal work behind her husband's judgment and her own decades of research training; no longitudinal novice-training evidence is supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Capability expansion is described as already occurring in April 2026; divergent cognitive outcomes and the training challenge are forward-looking without a specified horizon.
pts.d: Roberts's present-tense claims concern her current practice, illustrated by a collaboration two weeks before the article. Benefits are conditional on humans continuing to direct, question, edit and challenge outputs, and on genuinely performing higher-level thinking rather than letting AI do both detailed and strategic work. Existing expertise is presented as important to effective direction. The article specifies no date, adoption rate or magnitude for the predicted divergence or possible training crisis.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are researchers, writers and professional teams, with experienced supervisors and novices facing different opportunities and risks.
pts.d: Experienced researchers may broaden synthesis, explore unfamiliar disciplines and obtain on-demand critical dialogue. Professional team leaders, illustrated through legal supervision, may concentrate on strategy and editing while engaging less directly with underlying detail. Students and junior analysts may face difficulty acquiring foundational argument-building skills and judgment if AI allows them to bypass apprenticeship. Roberts also challenges binary authorship and originality assessments used by colleagues and educators. She makes no concrete claim about law-firm segments, pricing, client costs, access to justice or legal-market shares.
